changes.after: Tell the computer to show two lines of text in order.

before: A program is a sequence of instructions. Code is those instructions written in a language. This first program displays two pieces of text in order.
Text inside double quotes is a string: the quotes mark its boundaries and are not displayed. A statement is one instruction; a semicolon ends each output statement here.

#include <iostream> makes the standard input/output declarations available. int main() marks the program entry function, a named group of instructions: execution starts with the statements between its opening { and closing } braces.

std::cout is the standard output stream. Here << sends the following value to that stream. std:: selects a standard-library name. "\n" is a string containing a newline; it moves output onto the next line.
return 0; ends main with a success status for the operating system. It does not display 0. The int before main says that this function returns an integer, a whole-number value.

This course uses reading and understanding checks, not an in-browser compiler. The code is a complete optional local example. A compiler translates source code into a form a runtime or computer can execute.

For optional local work with GCC installed, save the example as main.cpp. In a terminal in that folder, run g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic main.cpp -o tiny, then run ./tiny on Linux or macOS. These are terminal commands, not C++ statements. Windows setup and executable launch differ. No game engine is required.
after: A program is a set of instructions for a computer to follow. Code is those instructions written in a programming language. Here, that language is C++.
A string is text. Double quotes mark the text in this example; the quotes are not displayed. A statement is an instruction, and a semicolon ends each output statement here.
The program starts in main, a function containing instructions. Its braces group those instructions. #include <iostream> makes the library names needed for text input and output available.
std::cout is the standard output stream, where the program sends its output. Here, << sends it a value. std:: chooses a name from the standard library. The text \n means a new line.
The int before main says this function returns a whole number. return 0 ends main with a success status for the operating system, the software that manages the computer. It does not print zero.
The program prints Start, then Explore on the next line. Each output statement sends text followed by a new line.

The browser shows C++ but does not run it. A compiler turns source code into a program you can run. For optional local work with GCC, save main.cpp and run g++ -std=c++23 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic main.cpp -o tiny in its folder. Run ./tiny on Linux or macOS, or .\tiny.exe in Windows PowerShell.

before: Read one small idea at a time.
Choose an answer and explain why.
Follow the statements in order with the changed value.
after: Read the output statements from top to bottom.

before.question: If the two output statements instead contain "Moon" first and "Sun" second, what is displayed?
choices: Moon then Sun, on separate lines.
Sun then Moon, because the last statement runs first.
The quote marks and instruction names, rather than the text.
before.explanation: Output statements run in sequence. Each writes its text then a newline; quote marks are code boundaries, not displayed characters.

after.question: Change the first word to "Moon" and the second to "Sun". What appears?
choices: Moon, then Sun on the next line
Sun, then Moon on the next line
The quote marks and instruction names
after.explanation: The output statements run in order. Quotes mark the text but do not appear in the output.
